nameStory: The bicoloured bracket gets its name from the striking two-toned appearance of its fruiting body. The 'bi' means two, and you'll often see distinct color zones or layers that make this fungus look like nature painted it with two different brushes. The 'bracket' part refers to how it grows like a shelf or bracket jutting out from dead wood.
description: The bicoloured bracket is a shelf-like fungus that grows directly from dead hardwood trees and logs. It forms tough, leathery brackets that can range from a few inches to over a foot across. True to its name, it displays distinct color zones - often showing bands of different browns, grays, or even orangish tones. The underside has tiny pores instead of gills, and the whole fungus feels firm and woody to the touch.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Shelf-like bracket with distinct color zones or bands, ranging from brown to gray to orange tones. Surface feels tough and leathery, sometimes with a slight velvety texture when young.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny, round pores rather than gills. Pore surface is typically white to cream colored and may bruise slightly when pressed.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels woody and tough, not spongy or soft like some other bracket fungi. Difficult to break or tear by hand.

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from dead wood with no stem, attached broadly to the substrate like a shelf or bracket.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Usually has a mild, pleasant mushroomy odor or no distinct smell. Not unpleasant or strong.

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: This species is inedible and too tough to eat. Never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification - some bracket fungi can be toxic.

habitat: Look for bicoloured brackets on dead hardwood trees and fallen logs in New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They're particularly common on oak, maple, and beech trees. You'll find them from lowland forests up to mid-elevation slopes, often in areas where there's plenty of decaying wood.

seasonality.spring: Fresh brackets may begin forming on newly dead wood. Look for younger specimens with more vibrant colors and softer textures.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when new brackets expand and mature. Colors are often most distinct during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Brackets continue to develop and older specimens become more woody. Fall rains can trigger new growth spurts.
seasonality.winter: Brackets persist year-round as tough, woody shelves. Older specimens may fade in color but remain identifiable by their bracket form and pore structure.

funFact: Despite being called 'bicoloured,' this bracket fungus can actually display three or more distinct color zones as it ages, creating natural artwork that changes throughout its lifetime - like tree rings but on the outside!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bracket fungi, but the distinct color banding helps separate it from uniform-colored species. Remember: 'bicoloured bands' - if you see clear color zones or bands across the cap surface, you're likely looking at this species rather than a solid-colored bracket.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name went through several changes over the years, and what mycologists once thought were separate species turned out to be the same fungus in different forms. This is common in fungus identification - the same species can look quite different depending on age and growing conditions.
compareHints: The bicoloured bracket differs from its relative, the green porecrust, by its much more substantial bracket-like growth form and distinct color banding. While green porecrust forms thinner, more crust-like growths, bicoloured bracket creates thick, woody shelves. The color zones are also much more pronounced in bicoloured bracket compared to the more uniform appearance of other Gloeoporus species.
